title: Mobile song, Calypso in Nassau and a planned trip home
summary: Mason links Mobile to a sailors' song heard in Nassau, describes Calypso and the bonefish song, and discusses his last visit to Miami and his planned return to Nassau.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Then, let's see, Baton Rouge and Donisonville, but never, never in a, never played in Mobile. I remember about Mobile, I was always, always intrigued about Mobile because when I was a boy down in Nassau, I'd go down to the wharf, down to the wharf when the ship's coming, I had a sailor sing a song, I saw the prettiest girl I ever saw down in Mobile. That was the song the sailors used to be, was famous among the sailors at that time. I saw the prettiest girl I ever saw down in Mobile. Funny thing, it was kind of funny, I married a girl from Mobile.
But you never did go there except through there? Never did go there, just passed through there. What kind of songs did you hear when you were a child?

Well, they call them Calypso now. They call them Calypso songs now, but they used to make them up around that song when I was a little fella. They are just like they do now, but of course nobody paid any attention to them. I remember one that used to sing about the bonefish, it used to call the bonefish song. Every man had his own bonefish. They just make them up like they went along? Oh yeah, that's just the way they do it. I guess it's like everything else. There was some people who was just cut out for that kind of stuff, you know, and they just started singing, you know, and they just make those things up as they go and would make it up on anything. The bonefish, of course, is a popular fish that they caught around there, but in this case where they speak of bonefish, they talk about that just like a man speak of his girlfriend. That's what that bonefish meant. Oh yeah. Everything meant something else. Everything meant something else. That's what they said. Yeah. However, I'm hoping to take a trip down to Nassau in about a couple of, maybe a couple of months. You got your papers straightened out? Well, I got it straightened out now, just about. I got it straightened out and I'm expecting to make a trip. And I think when I come back, I will bring quite a few of those songs because there are quite a few of them. I saw that Jack Parr show here the other night, not long ago, that came from down there and they had some of those kids singing some of those new Calypso songs they had there, you know, and doing some of the different dances they have down there now. So I'm quite sure that I'll pick up on quite a few of them before when I go down and make this trip. That'll be the first time you've ever been back? First time.
I bet that'll be something, huh?

I bet so. It will. As a matter of fact, I'm quite sure I wouldn't know anything about the place now. I know I was down in Miami in 19, the last time I was in Miami was in 1916, I think. And when I got back there, the papers had a big writer up there about the homeboy coming back and I remember I played the solo on the stage down there with the show, Masters in the Cold, Cold Ground. And I got quite a reception on that. But I got down, when I got down there, here about a couple of months ago, I couldn't even recognize, didn't recognize no place down there because the cities when I was there, the only thing that was there was palmetto trees and a whole lot of sandy streets. Now all the palmetto trees are pulled up and everything is entirely different. I didn't know, didn't even know where my church is. The church I used to go to when I was there, St. Agnes Church, I didn't even know that isn't there anymore. They tore it down. They had housing projects on that piece of land.
